description: My team is filled with visionaries ready to win.
summary:
Jezero Delta Atlas is a survival map for the first crew to walk on Mars at Jezero Crater's western delta. NASA's public Mars maps are built for regional and global views; ours works at walking scale, about 10 metres per pixel, over an 11 by 7 km area.

It supports one mission, Jezero Pathfinder, with two objectives: find evidence of ancient microbial life, and assess whether the site can sustain human life. The crew drives a pressurised rover to five stops, from the Three Forks sample depot to the ravine near the Cheyava Falls find, with two tasks at each stop.

The atlas layers a real orbital image with crater hazards detected by our own Python model, real Perseverance photos at every stop, and modelled radiation, relief and texture layers. A route planner finds a path around the hazards and rates each leg's risk. The same mission runs on three linked screens: a helmet display, a tablet, and an Earth mission-control page that receives SOS alerts.

It matters because astronauts need one trusted screen that says where to go, what is dangerous, and what to do when they arrive.
details:
WHAT IT DOES: Jezero Delta Atlas is an interactive map and mission tool for a Marswalk at Jezero Crater's western delta. It shows the terrain, the hazards, the science stops and a safe route, and links the astronaut to teammates and to Earth.

HOW IT WORKS: The base map is a real orbital image from the CTX camera on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter at about 10 m per pixel. Our Python model (a matched filter plus a random-forest classifier) finds craters and gives each a position, size and confidence: 36 marks, 7 high-confidence. The mission has five stops with real Perseverance Navcam photos and ten tasks, one per objective at each stop. A route planner (A* search on 17 m cells) goes around high-confidence craters and rates every leg's risk. Radiation, relief and texture layers are modelled from the orbital image and a radiation baseline measured by Curiosity's RAD instrument; they are not direct measurements and the app labels them so. Three screens share a room code: a helmet display, a tablet, and an Earth mission-control page with chat and SOS.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT: A crew gets one screen that answers where to go, what is dangerous on the way, and what to do on arrival, and Earth sees the same picture.

TOOLS: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no build step; Python with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, OpenCV and Pillow; GitHub with automated checks. Claude, an AI assistant, helped with parts of the code, documentation and slides.

CREATIVITY: We combined automatic hazard detection, a risk-rated route, and helmet, tablet and Earth views of one mission, and we state our limits: crater marks are not human-checked and stop positions are accurate to about 500 m.

FACTORS CONSIDERED: astronaut safety first, working offline, honest labelling of real versus modelled data, and a mission a crew can finish in one day.
